pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–8 years

- **Topic:** Comparing and grouping rocks by properties

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS2 Science, Year 3 Rocks):** Pupils compare and group together different kinds of rocks on the basis of their appearance and simple physical properties.

- **Standards — US (NGSS 2-PS1-1 property-classification approach applied to rocks; supports 2-ESS1 Earth materials):** Observe and describe rocks' observable properties and sort them into groups.

- **Operational details:** This is an observe-test-and-classify concept. Children examine real rocks and describe observable properties — hardness, texture (rough/smooth), colour, grain size, whether it's shiny or dull, holds together or crumbles. The core skill is choosing a property and SORTING a collection by it, then re-sorting by a different property (the same rocks group differently depending on the criterion). Emphasise evidence-based description ('this one is harder because it scratches that one') and careful observation with hand lenses. Keep it about observable physical properties, not yet rock TYPE names (igneous/sedimentary come later); grouping precedes naming.
bestPractices: Use real rock specimens and hand lenses — grouping rocks is a hands-on observation task, not a picture-only one.
Have children choose a property, sort, then RE-SORT by a different property so they see grouping depends on the chosen criterion.
Insist on evidence-based comparison (a scratch test for hardness, rubbing for texture) rather than guessing.
Build precise property vocabulary: hardness, texture, grain size, colour, lustre (shiny/dull), whether it crumbles.
Keep the focus on observable properties before rock-type names — classification by evidence comes before taxonomy.
keyRepresentations: A rock collection with hand lenses for direct observation.
A property sorting mat / Venn hoops (e.g. 'rough' vs 'smooth', 'hard' vs 'crumbly').
A comparison table: rock × property (hardness, colour, grain, texture).
A scratch-test / rub-test station for evidence gathering.
commonMisconceptions: 'Rocks can only be sorted one right way' — not seeing that different properties give different valid groupings.
'All grey rocks are the same rock' — grouping by colour alone and ignoring texture/hardness.
'Bigger rocks are harder' — confusing size with hardness.
'You can tell a rock's properties just by looking' — skipping the test (scratch/rub) that gives evidence.

learn.summary: Children aged 7–8 learn to compare and group rocks by observable physical properties — hardness, texture (rough/smooth), colour, grain size, lustre (shiny/dull), and whether a rock crumbles. The central skill is choosing a property, sorting a collection by it, then RE-SORTING by a different property so learners discover that the same rocks group differently depending on the chosen criterion. Emphasis stays on evidence-based description ('this one is harder because it scratches that one') gathered with hands-on tests and hand lenses, and on observable properties rather than rock-type names (igneous/sedimentary come later): grouping precedes naming.

activities.title: Test, describe and sort a rock collection
feedback: If a learner sorts only by colour, ask: 'Two of these are both grey — how could you still tell them apart and put them in different groups?' Prompt a scratch or rub test.

When a learner claims a rock is harder, ask for the evidence: 'How did you test that?' Reinforce that a scratch test shows which rock scratches the other, so hardness is relative to the specimens compared (and to the tool, if a nail or coin is used). Check that the mark is a real scratch and not powder from the softer rock that rubs away.

After sorting by one property, invite the switch: 'Now sort the same rocks by hardness instead of colour — what happens to your groups?' Draw attention to the same rocks ending up in different groups.
If a learner assumes bigger rocks are harder, have them scratch-test a large soft rock against a small hard one to check directly — size and hardness are separate properties.
If a learner thinks shiny means precious or metal, note that lustre is just one observable property and ask what the scratch and texture tests show.
activities.rationale: The concept is observe-test-and-classify, so acting on real specimens — scratching, rubbing, tapping, lensing — then physically regrouping them makes the dependence of grouping on the chosen criterion visible through action. Classification by observable properties, with the same objects sortable multiple ways, is a foundational science practice named in the standards.
sourceClaims: DfE KS2 Year 3 Rocks: pupils compare and group together different kinds of rocks on the basis of their appearance and simple physical properties.
Classification by observable properties (hardness, texture, colour, grain) with the same objects sortable multiple ways is a foundational science-skills practice.
learnerActions: Examine a set of varied real rock specimens with a hand lens, looking closely at grain size and surface.

For each rock, carry out simple evidence-gathering tests: a scratch test for hardness (which rock scratches which), a rub test for texture (rough or smooth), a tap or gentle press to see whether it crumbles or holds together, and note colour and lustre (shiny or dull).
Record each rock's properties on a property card or a rock × property comparison table (hardness, colour, grain, texture).
Choose one property and sort the whole collection into groups (e.g. rough vs smooth, or hard vs crumbly), using sorting hoops/Venn hoops or a sorting mat.
Then re-sort the SAME rocks by a different property (e.g. switch from colour to hardness) and observe how the groups change.
State the evidence behind a comparison aloud, e.g. 'this one is harder because it scratched that one.'
activities.intendedInsight: A grouping depends on the property you choose: the same collection of rocks can fall into different groups when you sort by a different observable property, though some rocks may stay together. Describing rocks by tested evidence is more reliable than guessing by looking.

activities.title: Compare two contrasting rocks
feedback: If a learner says all rocks are the same, have them handle the varied set and feel the differences in hardness, texture and weight, and see the range of colours.
If a learner names only one property, prompt them to add another: 'You said the colour — what about how hard or rough each one is?'
Praise comparisons that cite a tested property rather than appearance alone. Keep weight and hardness distinct — a large rock can be soft and a small rock hard.
activities.rationale: Comparing a contrasting pair elicits precise property vocabulary and counters the idea that rocks are all alike; it directly targets the evidence of describing how two rocks' properties differ.
sourceClaims: DfE KS2 Year 3 Rocks: pupils compare and group together different kinds of rocks on the basis of their appearance and simple physical properties.
learnerActions: Take two clearly different rocks — for example one smooth, pale and crumbly, and one dark, heavy and very hard.
Describe how each differs across several properties: hardness, texture, colour, grain size and weight.
Decide and explain which group each rock would go into and why.
Answer: are all rocks basically the same, or can they be sorted into groups? Give evidence.
activities.intendedInsight: Rocks differ in several observable properties at once, so a single pair can be told apart and grouped in more than one way depending on which property you focus on.

activities.title: Is it really a rock?
feedback: If a learner counts a brick as a rock, point out that bricks and concrete are made by people while rocks form naturally.
Accept reasoning that distinguishes natural from manufactured rather than relying on hardness alone.
activities.rationale: The common misconception that manufactured hard materials are rocks is worth addressing directly so classification rests on 'natural rock' rather than 'hard thing'.
learnerActions: Look at everyday manufactured items alongside rock specimens (e.g. a brick, concrete, glass).
Decide whether each is a rock and give a reason.
Discuss what makes something a natural rock versus a material made by people.
activities.intendedInsight: Rocks are natural materials; bricks, concrete and manufactured glass (such as window or bottle glass) are made by people, often from rock materials, so they are not rocks even though they can be hard.

activities.title: Build observation vocabulary with a tap-to-reveal collection (supporting scaffold)
feedback: Confirm correct matches of rock to property and discuss any mismatches by returning to the observable feature.
When ordering rocks by hardness, ask what evidence (a scratch test) would confirm the order.
activities.rationale: A reveal-and-match collection builds the observation vocabulary that the hands-on sorting relies on, and matching/ordering/categorising let classification be checked cleanly. Its limit is that the property evidence is supplied rather than tested by the learner, so it supports but does not replace doing the tests and the re-sorting.
sourceClaims: Classification by observable properties (hardness, texture, colour, grain) with the same objects sortable multiple ways is a foundational science-skills practice.
learnerActions: Tap each specimen in a rock collection to reveal a property fact-card (hardness, texture, colour) and a lens zoom on the grain.
Use a lift-the-flap prompt: 'Which group would you put this in?' and choose a group before revealing.
Practise matching a rock to a property description and sequencing rocks by hardness.
activities.intendedInsight: Precise property vocabulary (hardness, texture, grain size, colour, lustre) lets you describe and compare rocks accurately.

constraints: Rocks are physical specimens: a real box of rocks with hand lenses and a scratch-test kit is the essential hands-on complement. The specific picture-only or tap-to-reveal formats described here supply the property evidence and support vocabulary/recognition; they do not elicit the learner's own physical testing or the re-sort-by-a-new-criterion that drives the concept — the recommended simulated bench and the real specimens provide that.
Keep the focus on observable physical properties before introducing rock-type names (igneous/sedimentary); grouping by evidence comes before taxonomy.

Insist on evidence-based comparison (scratch test for hardness, rubbing for texture) rather than guessing from appearance; present hardness as relative ('which scratches which'), since outcomes depend on the specimens and tool.
Matching, ordering and categorising tasks check classification but supply the property evidence; they assess recognition rather than eliciting the learner's own testing and re-sorting.

Rotating a 3D specimen can add observational realism (seeing texture on all sides before sorting) but the core learning is property-testing and sorting logic, not spatial manipulation; treat 3D as an optional enhancement, not a requirement.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Both cited sources are marked verified:false in the source row; treat the standards citations as unconfirmed.

The original framed a conversation/dialogue format as unable to substitute for hands-on observation. This has been softened: dialogue is simply not the chosen format here because the task is hands-on testing and sorting; no universal claim about dialogue's teaching ability is asserted.

The source assessment lists 'Bigger rocks are harder' as a misconception but the response-levels/diagnostic emphasise weight as a describable property — weight and hardness are distinct; keep them separate in teaching (a large rock can be soft, a small rock hard).

Scratch-test outcomes depend on the specific specimens and the tool used (e.g. a nail); real results vary by material, so present relative hardness ('which scratches which') rather than absolute claims.
A prerequisite reteach link is referenced for the 'all rocks are the same' misconception; the prerequisite linkage is not independently verified in this rewrite (internal identifier omitted).

probeDeeper: Is a brick a rock? Why or why not?
Two rocks are both grey. How could you still tell them apart and put them in different groups?
How would you test which of two rocks is harder?
assess.correctAnswer: Rocks are not all the same — they differ in observable properties, so we can group them. You can describe and sort by hardness (does it scratch easily?), texture (smooth or rough, grainy), colour, grain size and weight. Sorting by a chosen property puts similar rocks together.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'All rocks are basically the same (hard and grey)'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Handle a varied set — feel hardness, texture and weight, see the range of colours.
errorPatterns.distractor: Rocks are all the same, so you can't really sort them.

errorPatterns.nextMove: Rocks are natural; bricks and concrete are made by people.
errorPatterns.distractor: A brick is a kind of rock.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'You can only sort rocks by colour'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce a scratch test and a texture feel as other properties.

responseLevels.gap: Says all rocks are the same, or that a brick is a rock; sorts only by colour.
responseLevels.full: Describes several observable properties (hardness, texture, colour, grain), sorts a collection by a chosen property, distinguishes natural rock from made materials, and compares two rocks' properties.
responseLevels.partial: Names a couple of properties and sorts, but leans on colour alone or includes manufactured materials.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are two rocks: one is smooth, pale and crumbly; the other is dark, heavy and very hard. Are all rocks basically the same, or can we sort them into groups? What could you look at or test to describe and group them?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks 'a rock is just a rock,' or who judges only by colour, differs from one who names several observable properties and uses one to group.
